group: Unit i — RRTS / High Speed Operations
title: Fundamentals of RRTS Operations & Train Operating Procedures

questions.q: In Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS), 'Operations' means:
options: Only the maintenance of trains in the depot
The safe, punctual, passenger-focused running of trains and stations as one system, to a single plan — the timetable
questions.explain: Operations = trains, tracks, signalling, power, stations, staff and information all moving to the timetable.

questions.q: Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) is best described as:
options: An open system shared with freight trains
A loco-hauled system with level crossings
A tram system running on roads
A closed, fully grade-separated, high-frequency Electric Multiple Unit (EMU) system with no level crossings and no mixed freight traffic
questions.explain: No level crossings, no freight, fixed trainsets — that is why headways of a few minutes are possible.

questions.q: EMU stands for:
options: Electric Multiple Unit — motorised coaches distributed along the train, with no separate locomotive
Electric Main Unit — one engine coach only
questions.explain: In an Electric Multiple Unit (EMU), traction motors are spread through the coaches, so no separate locomotive is needed.

questions.q: In operations language, a 'rake' or 'trainset' means:
options: A single spare coach in the depot
The crew roster for one shift
The fixed formation of coaches that runs as one train
questions.explain: Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) runs fixed trainsets/rakes rather than daily re-formed loco trains.

questions.q: Headway means:
options: The time a train stands at a platform
The time interval between two successive trains at a point
The height of the overhead wire
questions.explain: Headway is the gap between trains; dwell is the standing time at a platform — the pair is always asked together.

questions.q: Dwell time means:
options: The time a train stands at a platform for boarding and alighting
The time to reverse at a terminal
questions.explain: Dwell = platform standing time for passenger exchange.

questions.q: Turnaround time means:
options: The time a train stands at an intermediate platform
The time taken at a terminal to reverse a train for its return trip
questions.explain: Turnaround is the terminal reversal time; minimum turnaround is vital in peak hours.

questions.q: Revenue service means:
options: An empty run from depot to the first station
Train running that carries passengers as per the timetable
A train parked in the depot
questions.explain: Revenue service = passenger-carrying service. Empty depot runs are non-revenue movements.

questions.q: Which of these is a NON-revenue movement?
options: An empty run from the depot to the starting station
questions.explain: Non-revenue = no passengers carried, e.g. depot transfers, empty runs and trials — but full safety rules still apply.

questions.q: Stabling means:
options: Running a train at full speed
Holding a train at a station
Parking a train at a depot or stabling line when not in service
questions.explain: Stabled trains are parked, e.g. overnight, until their next duty.

questions.q: Shunting means:
options: Planned movement of trains/coaches within a depot or yard
Emergency braking on the main line
questions.explain: Shunting is controlled movement inside depot/yard limits, not main-line running.

questions.q: A possession is:
options: Ownership of a train by the operator
Protected, authorised access to a track area for work, with trains excluded
questions.explain: Possession gives maintenance protected track access — normally in non-revenue hours.

questions.q: The train operations cycle begins with:
options: Train preparation in the depot — checks, cleaning, testing brakes, doors and radio
questions.explain: Cycle order: preparation → induction → revenue running → turnaround → withdrawal → examination/maintenance handover.

questions.q: After revenue running and terminal turnaround, a train is:
options: Withdrawn to the depot/stabling and handed over for examination and maintenance
questions.explain: Withdrawal and maintenance handover close the daily operations cycle.

questions.q: 'Induction' of a train means:
options: Bringing a prepared train from the depot into revenue service
questions.explain: Induction = entering service; withdrawal = leaving service.

questions.q: In Automatic Train Operation (ATO), the Train Operator's main job is to:
options: Drive every movement fully by hand
Supervise the automatic running, manage doors, and handle degraded/emergency actions
questions.explain: Automatic Train Operation (ATO) drives; the operator supervises, controls doors and takes over when things go wrong.

questions.q: Before taking duty, train crew must be:
options: Only medically fit; route knowledge is optional
Route-competent, rule-competent and medically fit, with prescribed rest taken
Fresh from any other full shift
questions.explain: Competency, medical fitness and rostered rest are all compulsory for train crew.

questions.q: Prescribed rest before duty for train crew is governed by:
questions.explain: Rosters are built so crew get their prescribed rest and stay competency-compliant.

questions.q: The first law of operations is:
options: 'No authority = no movement' — every movement needs an authority, a defined route and a safe speed
questions.explain: Authority from signalling and the Operations Control Centre (OCC), a set route and a safe speed must all exist before any movement.

questions.q: A Permanent Speed Restriction (PSR) exists because of:
questions.explain: Permanent Speed Restrictions (PSRs) are built into the design; Temporary Speed Restrictions (TSRs) come from temporary conditions.

questions.q: A Temporary Speed Restriction (TSR) is imposed because of:
options: The permanent design of a curve
Work or a defect for a limited period, notified to crew and Operations Control Centre (OCC)
questions.explain: Temporary Speed Restrictions (TSRs) are temporary, condition-based, and must be notified to crew and Operations Control Centre (OCC).

questions.q: Overspeeding by a train is prevented by:
questions.explain: Automatic Train Protection (ATP) supervises speed and stops the train from exceeding the safe limit.

questions.q: Punctuality of trains is measured:
options: Once a month from ticket sales
Against the timetable at timing points
questions.explain: Right-time running is checked at defined timing points along the route.

questions.q: A small delay can be recovered by:
options: Reduced dwell (within safe limits), timetable recovery margins, and Operations Control Centre (OCC) regulation decisions
Closing the Platform Screen Doors (PSDs) early
questions.explain: Recovery uses safe tools only — dwell discipline, built-in margins and regulation; never unsafe speed.

questions.q: The Working Timetable is:
options: The master plan of every train — timings, routes, platform allocation and depot in/out movements
questions.explain: The working timetable is the day's operational master plan.

questions.q: The Duty Roster tells:
options: Who works which train/station shift, with rest and competency compliance
questions.explain: Roster = people plan; working timetable = train plan.

questions.q: Notices and circulars issued before duty mainly communicate:
options: Temporary Speed Restrictions (TSRs), engineering work and special instructions for the day, to be briefed before duty
questions.explain: Crews must be briefed on the day's Temporary Speed Restrictions (TSRs), works and special instructions before starting.

questions.q: Before the first train of the day, which readiness items are confirmed?
options: Trains, signalling, power, Platform Screen Doors (PSDs), radio and Automatic Fare Collection (AFC)/Passenger Information System (PIS)
questions.explain: Pre-service readiness covers every system the first train depends on.

questions.q: The three operating states of a train are:
options: Revenue service, non-revenue movement and stabling
questions.explain: A train is either carrying passengers, moving empty, or stabled (parked).

questions.q: 'Roll-out' means:
options: Trains leaving the depot to enter revenue service
Trains returning to the depot after service
questions.explain: Roll-out = depot to service in the morning; roll-in = back to depot.

questions.q: 'Roll-in' means:
options: Trains leaving the depot for service
Trains returning to the depot after finishing service
questions.explain: Roll-in completes the daily cycle before the night maintenance window.

questions.q: Which are the driving modes mentioned for Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) trains?
options: Automatic Train Operation (ATO), Automatic Train Protection (ATP)-manual and RM (Restricted Manual), as the system permits
questions.explain: Modes range from Automatic Train Operation (ATO) down to Restricted Manual, used as conditions permit.

questions.q: Door interlocking ensures that:
options: Doors open while the train is moving
A train cannot move with a door open
Passengers can force doors at speed
Platform Screen Doors (PSDs) open before the train stops
questions.explain: Interlock: doors proved closed and locked before traction is possible.

questions.q: Berthing accuracy at Platform Screen Door (PSD) stations matters because:
options: Train doors must align exactly with the Platform Screen Doors
questions.explain: If the train stops off-mark, its doors will not match the Platform Screen Doors (PSDs) and boarding cannot happen normally.

questions.q: If a Train Operator receives an instruction that would clearly endanger safety, he must:
options: Refuse it, protect the train, and report it to Operations Control Centre (OCC)/supervisor
questions.explain: No instruction overrides safety — refuse, protect, report. This is tested in every metro operations paper.

questions.q: Written operating procedures are important mainly because:
options: They replace the need for training
They make every crew, on every shift, do the same job the same safe way — memory fails under pressure, a checklist does not
questions.explain: Like pilots' checklists, procedures remove dependence on individual memory.

questions.q: A train's trip refers to:
options: One scheduled run of a train between its start and end points
questions.explain: Each scheduled run in the timetable is a trip.

questions.q: A block section is:
options: A defined length of track protected so that train movements within it are controlled by authority/signalling
A ticket block in the booking office
questions.explain: Movements enter a block section only with authority — part of the 'no authority = no movement' rule.

questions.q: Right-time, right-direction working matters because:
options: It is only a slogan for posters
Trains must run to the timetable on their correct line/direction for the planned service to be safe and punctual
questions.explain: Correct direction and timing keep the single plan — the timetable — intact for the whole line.

questions.q: Peak-hour working needs:
options: Maximum fleet deployment and minimum turnaround time
Only spare trains in the depot
questions.explain: Peak demand is met by putting the maximum trains out and turning them round fastest.

questions.q: A 'caution order' handed to a train crew before departure mainly tells them about:
options: Their leave roster for the month
Speed restrictions and special conditions to observe on the run ahead
The fare chart for the route
questions.explain: A caution order is a written warning listing every speed restriction and unusual condition on the trip, so the crew is never surprised by a restriction ahead.

questions.q: 'Berthing' a train at a station means:
options: Parking it in the depot for the night
Bringing it to a stop at the exact marked position on the platform
Taking it out of service for washing
questions.explain: Berthing is stopping precisely at the platform stopping mark, so the train doors align with the Platform Screen Doors (PSDs) and passengers can board safely.

questions.q: The very first train after the night maintenance block is normally run cautiously because it also serves to:
options: Prove the section is clear of men, material and obstructions before normal service
questions.explain: After night work, the first train acts as a proving run — it confirms the track is clear and fit before full-speed passenger service begins.

questions.q: A train's event recorder (its 'black box') is fitted mainly to:
options: Record speed, braking and other running data for later analysis and investigation
questions.explain: The event recorder logs how the train was driven — speed, brake use, door events — so any incident can be reconstructed factually afterwards.

questions.q: A train is detained at a stop signal for several minutes with no authority to move. The Train Operator should FIRST:
options: Open the doors so passengers can get down
Inform the Operations Control Centre (OCC), follow its instructions and keep passengers informed
Reverse the train to the previous station on his own
Leave the cab and walk to the signal
questions.explain: On detention, the operator reports to the Operations Control Centre (OCC) at once and waits for instructions; unauthorised moves or detraining passengers on the track can create a bigger danger.
